flashcard_questions.a: The dynamic external system in which a business competes and functions.
Rival businesses repeatedly lower their prices to undercut each other.
Businesses selling the same type of product to the same target market.
Businesses selling different products but competing for the same customer spending.
A planning tool that sets internal strengths and weaknesses against external opportunities and threats.

flashcard_questions.q: Which half of a SWOT analysis covers factors outside the business?
How does Burger King differentiate itself from McDonald's?
flashcard_questions.a: It flame-grills its burgers instead of frying them.

flashcard_questions.q: Which factor does Aldi mainly compete on against Tesco?
Why do Greggs and Costa locate on high streets and near stations?
flashcard_questions.a: To catch grab-and-go customers where footfall is high.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do IKEA and B&Q choose retail parks instead of high streets?
flashcard_questions.a: There is space for large stores and free parking.

flashcard_questions.q: How often does Zara refresh its fashion lines to keep customers returning?
Which loyalty card does Tesco use to encourage repeat purchases?
Why is keeping a customer cheaper than winning a new one?
flashcard_questions.a: Selling to an existing customer costs the business less.
Placing customer satisfaction at the heart of every business decision.

flashcard_questions.q: When has a business added value for a customer?
flashcard_questions.a: When the customer sees extra benefit and is prepared to pay more.

notes: 15 cards: 6 term→definition (competitive environment, price war, direct, indirect, SWOT, customer orientated), 6 concept→named example (Burger King, Aldi, Greggs/Costa, IKEA/B&Q, Zara, Tesco Clubcard), 2 single-fact advantage cards, 1 added-value card. The five competitive factors were not made into one list card — enumeration answers break Rule 2.
